task_instruction: Compose a formal grant summary for reconciling historic tithe maps with modern spatial datasets.
task_details: Provide a tightly written paragraph for a funding application describing objectives, Deliverables:, Outputs include..., a measurable indicator (number of tithe parcels georeferenced), timeline (within 9 months), budget stated as 'costed at £...', methods (georeferencing, attribute reconciliation, EPSG:27700), intended users, and data publication/licensing plan.
personalized: Objectives: To reconcile historic tithe apportionments with current cadastral boundaries and produce a fully georeferenced, searchable dataset to support heritage research and rural planning. Deliverables: Georeferenced tithe map tiles, a harmonised attribute table linking apportionment references to modern parcel identifiers, and documentation specifying methods and uncertainties. Outputs include at least 6,000 tithe parcels georeferenced to EPSG:27700 with provenance metadata and a downloadable GeoPackage. If funded, we will complete digitisation, georeferencing and attribute reconciliation within 9 months and publish the dataset under a permissive open licence. Costed at £22,400, the budget covers archival access, specialist digitisation, QA/QC and metadata creation. Impact on communities will be measured through use by local heritage groups and planners; expected immediate outputs include three community seminars and one policy note for conservation officers. Risks include illegible apportionments and inconsistent historical place-names; mitigation will use cross-referencing with tithe apportionments and local oral-history verification where available.

task_instruction: Create a formal pitch for mapping hedgerows and field-boundary networks for biodiversity planning.
task_details: Write a compact funding paragraph that states project aim, Objectives:, Deliverables:, Outputs include..., technical approach (LiDAR canopy/CHM, field validation), measurable outputs (kilometres of hedgerow mapped), timeline (within 12 months), precise budget 'costed at £...', intended impacts on farming communities and biodiversity officers, and risk mitigation.
personalized: Objectives: To map hedgerow and field-boundary networks across a 150 km2 rural catchment to inform biodiversity corridors and agri-environment planning. Deliverables: LiDAR-derived canopy height and linear feature extraction, validated hedgerow vector dataset at 1:5,000 scale, and a technical guidance note for integration into farm stewardship plans. Outputs include mapping of at least 450 kilometres of hedgerow features with associated condition and continuity attributes, and a GeoPackage suitable for local authority and farm advisor use. If funded, we will complete remote-sensing analysis and ground-truthing within 12 months. Costed at £36,000, the budget includes LiDAR processing, three weeks of field survey, stakeholder engagement with farming groups and production of guidance. Impact on communities will include improved targeting of agri-environment funds and clearer advice for landowners; performance indicators include number of hedgerow features incorporated into stewardship applications. Risks include seasonal visibility constraints; these will be managed by scheduling field validation outside leaf-on extremes and by using multi-season imagery where available.

task_instruction: Draft a formal funding paragraph for a volunteer training programme in community GIS and data stewardship.
task_details: Produce a concise formal paragraph aimed at a grant panel describing objectives, Deliverables:, Outputs include..., training methods (QField, QGIS), measurable targets (number of volunteers trained, volunteer hours), timeline (within 12 months), budget 'costed at £...', supervision and sustainability plan, and risk mitigation for data quality.
personalized: Objectives: To establish a community data stewardship scheme that trains local volunteers in mobile data collection (QField) and desktop GIS (QGIS) to maintain and update rural settlement datasets. Deliverables: A curriculum of five modular training sessions, training materials and a cohort of accredited volunteers capable of routine audits. Outputs include training of at least 12 volunteers, 480 volunteer hours logged within 12 months and quarterly data updates committed to the central GeoPackage. If funded, we will deliver the training programme, supervise initial fieldwork and provide ongoing remote QA support within 12 months. Costed at £14,800, the budget covers instructor time, training licences where needed, equipment hire and participant support. Impact on communities will be measured by increased local involvement in mapping and by the number of dataset updates driven by volunteers. Risks include variability in volunteer retention and data quality; mitigation comprises formal accreditation steps, standardised data collection forms and routine QA by the project team.

task_instruction: Write a formal proposal paragraph for creating an emergency routing dataset for rural access by services.
task_details: Provide a tightly written paragraph for a grant panel outlining project Objectives:, Deliverables:, Outputs include..., technical methods (network analysis, axle/load restrictions, weight limits), measurable outcomes (reduction in response time or identified bottlenecks), timeline (within 12 months), budget 'costed at £...', stakeholder engagement with emergency services and councils, and risk mitigation steps.
personalized: Objectives: To produce a validated emergency-access routing layer for narrow lanes and rural track networks to improve response times and logistical planning for emergency services. Deliverables: A routable GIS network with encoded restrictions (width, weight, surface), a mobile-compatible map layer for first responders and a short integration guide for council GIS teams. Outputs include identification of 320 lane impediments and a routable dataset that can be consumed by emergency dispatch systems. If funded, we will complete field verification, construct the network and deliver training to emergency planners within 12 months. Costed at £55,000, the project budget covers detailed field surveys, specialist network modelling and stakeholder workshops with fire, ambulance and council highways officers. Impact on communities will be measured by a reduction in identified access bottlenecks and by uptake of the layer in emergency plans; a target is a measurable improvement in route reliability for at least five priority incident types. Risks include legacy address data that is not routable; mitigation will involve cross-referencing OS address data and local knowledge to ensure accurate geocoding.

task_instruction: Draft a formal funding pitch for developing a prioritisation tool for small-scale rural infrastructure investment.
task_details: Write a concise formal paragraph for a grant panel describing Objectives:, Deliverables:, Outputs include..., methodology (multi-criteria analysis, GIS model), measurable outputs (ranked list of interventions, number of scenarios), timeline (within 6 months), budget 'costed at £...', integration plan with council decision-making, and risk mitigation for data gaps.

Outputs include generation of at least three investment scenarios and a ranked list of 50 candidate projects with quantified scores and cost estimates. If funded, we will deliver the tool and training to the regional planning team within 6 months. Costed at £42,500, the budget covers model development, stakeholder workshops and integration support. Impact on communities will be measured by improved allocation of capital budgets and by the number of projects progressed through council decision cycles; immediate indicators include adoption of the tool in at least one council capital programme. Risks include incomplete baseline data; mitigation will include sensitivity testing and conservative default values where data are missing, with clear documentation of assumptions.

task_instruction: Email to volunteers expressing thanks and providing dataset link with next steps.
task_details: Draft a friendly email to volunteer field surveyors and local history contributors thanking them, linking to the dataset DOI/URL and download page, summarising what is included (attributes, formats, EPSG), explaining how volunteers can suggest edits, and proposing a small celebratory walk or debrief event. personalized: Hi all, Thanks to everyone for the time, patience and local knowledge you put into the hamlet surveys. Open data now available at DOI/URL https://doi.org/10.5285/hamlets-cornwall-2026 with downloads and metadata at https://data.truro.ac.uk/hamlets. The package includes point features for hamlet centres, a polygon layer for extents, attribute fields for historical names and source notes, and GeoJSON and shapefile exports in EPSG:27700. task_details: Compose a short press-style announcement for a local newspaper about the dataset publication. personalized: A new open dataset returning tiny settlements and traditional place-names to regional maps has been published today. The hamlet mapping project used historic tithe plans, aerial imagery and on-the-ground surveys to produce an accessible dataset for local people and planners. Open data now available at DOI/URL https://doi.org/10.5285/hamlets-cornwall-2026. The project was supported by the county council and the Heritage Fund and involved dozens of volunteers. As Nell Davies, who led the mapping, explains: It’s been brilliant to see names that people remembered but that no longer appear on modern maps come back into use. We’re holding a free drop-in workshop at the community hall next month to show the maps and discuss how to use the data. Thanks to everyone who helped. Please do reuse and share.

personalized: Title: Rural Hamlet and Historic Place-Name Dataset, Cornwall. Thanks to the parish councils, the county heritage group and all volunteer surveyors who made this possible. Really pleased with this; please do reuse and share.

Frequently uses lists or numbered steps in technical notes and emails to make actions explicit; keeps passive voice to a minimum except when emphasising procedures or standards. Parenthetical clarifications (e.g. OS grid, EPSG codes) and inline examples are common to aid reproducibility.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Mixes technical GIS and cartographic vocabulary with local rural terminology: e.g. 'shapefile', 'feature class', 'attribute table', 'EPSG:27700 / OS grid', 'orthophoto', 'LiDAR', 'ground-truth', plus local terms like 'hamlet', 'tithe map', 'hedgerow', 'lane', 'pasties' and 'cider'. Prefers clear, Anglo-British phrasing and metric units (metres, kilometres); will cite map scales (1:25,000), grid refs (SX123456) or GPS waypoints when precise location matters. Uses software-specific terms when talking to peers (ArcGIS Pro, QField, QGIS) but explains jargon for community audiences.
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of polite hedges and pragmatic markers: 'I'd suggest', 'worth flagging', 'if possible' and 'best to check'. Uses contractions in informal communication ('I'm', 'we'll', 'it's') and discourse cues like 'on the ground', 'to be honest' and 'that said' to signal shifts in emphasis. Example phrases: 'On the ground it's usually…', 'Worth flagging that…', 'If you're happy with that, I'll…', and 'best to check the tithe/apportionment first.'

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: A celebratory, public-facing post sharing a newly published open dataset or completed community mapping project, thanking volunteers and partners.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Warm, modestly celebratory and community-centred; emphasises collaboration, gives clear links to the resource and credits contributors. Uses short praise sentences, inclusive language and a gentle invitation for reuse or further involvement.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: "Thanks to everyone", "open data now available", "DOI/URL" and "loving seeing local names returned to the map". Use appreciative short sentences ("Really pleased with this."), name-check partners politely, and include simple calls to action ("Please do reuse and share"). Maintain humility while signalling achievement, and use phrases that reflect local pride and collective effort.

Keep tone cordial and community-centred.
